rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 and Tables 1-3 report a two-year randomized block field experiment in Nadia, West Bengal comparing surface irrigation with gravity drip and micro-sprinkler at 1.0 and 0.7 of pan evaporation on broccoli and cauliflower, measuring soil and head arsenic, yield, water use, water productivity, antioxidant enzymes and economics.
rows.notes: The study tests gravity-fed drip and micro-sprinkler irrigation scheduled by Class A pan evaporation, not app-based or smart irrigation scheduling; no software, sensor or decision-support tool is involved. Its own results are water saving (up to 37.3%), higher water productivity, reduced arsenic accumulation in edible heads (5-17%), modest yield gains and lower dietary carcinogenic risk under micro-irrigation versus surface irrigation (Tables 1-2, Figs. 1 and 5). It does not evaluate climate-change adaptation, resilience or risk management as an outcome. Water-saving results are reported as pooled means with SEm/LSD for yield and As but not for water use. The conclusion notes applicability is limited for rice and calls for up-scaling to diverse physiographic locations.

notes: Full text appears complete. The review cites this study as an example of water-saving/smart irrigation for climate adaptation; the study is a primary field trial of conventional drip and sprinkler micro-irrigation for arsenic mitigation and water productivity, with no app or smart scheduling component and no climate-risk outcome.
